html:
The 1939 Erzincan earthquake struck eastern Turkey in the early hours of 27 December 1939. With a magnitude of about 7.8 it is tied with the 2023 earthquakes as the strongest recorded in the country. About 33,000 people died.

The city of Erzincan was almost flattened, and many villages around it were destroyed. It was midwinter, with snow and severe cold, and many survivors died of exposure before help arrived, and snow blocked roads and slowed rescue.

The quake ruptured a long stretch of the North Anatolian Fault, where the Anatolian plate slides west past the Eurasian plate. It began a series of large quakes that moved westward along the fault over the following decades, a pattern that led up to the 1999 Izmit earthquake near Istanbul. The city was rebuilt on a new site a little to the north.
